Scab
SKAB
noun
From the Old English sceabb and Old Norse skabb, a crust or roughness upon the skin; kin to the adjective shabby. In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew sappachath and mispachath, the scaly eruption which the priest was commanded to examine under the law of the plague of leprosy.

Biblical Definition

A scab is a scaly eruption of the skin, and in Leviticus 13 it is the very thing the priest was appointed to look upon. The law did not tell the Israelite to judge his own flesh. “When a man shall have in the skin of his flesh a rising, a scab, or bright spot, and it be in the skin of his flesh like the plague of leprosy; then he shall be brought unto Aaron the priest” (Lev 13:2). He was brought. He did not diagnose himself, and he did not take a vote of his neighbours; he stood before the appointed examiner and waited on the verdict. The priest shut him up seven days and looked again, and if the plague spread not, “the priest shall pronounce him clean: it is but a scab” (Lev 13:6). But if it spread, the sentence was the other way: “it is a leprosy” (Lev 13:8). Two men might carry the same mark and receive opposite verdicts, and the difference was not in the man’s opinion of himself but in what the plague did over time under a lawful eye. Isaiah turns the word upon the proud: “the Lord will smite with a scab the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion” (Isa 3:17), where the ornament was, there the sore shall be. So the scab in Scripture is the small beginning that must be examined, because a spot which spreads is no longer a spot.

Webster 1828 Definition

An incrusted substance, dry and rough, formed over a sore in healing; a mangy or scaly eruption of the skin; the itch.

expand to see more

SCAB, an incrustation or crust of dried matter formed over a wound or sore in the process of healing.

The itch or mange in animals; a scaly or crusted eruption upon the skin of man.

From Saxon sceabb; allied to Old Norse skabb, and to the Latin scabies, roughness, from scabo, to scratch.

In the Levitical law the scab is the symptom the priest examines and re-examines before he pronounces clean or unclean (Lev 13:2–8).

Figuratively, a small and superficial defilement which may prove to be a deep and spreading one.

Key Scripture

Lev 13:2 — "When a man shall have in the skin of his flesh a rising, a scab, or bright spot, and it be in the skin of his flesh like the plague of leprosy; then he shall be brought unto Aaron the priest, or unto one of his sons the priests:"

Lev 13:6 — "And the priest shall look on him again the seventh day: and, behold, if the plague be somewhat dark, and the plague spread not in the skin, the priest shall pronounce him clean: it is but a scab: and he shall wash his clothes, and be clean."

Lev 13:8 — "And if the priest see that, behold, the scab spreadeth in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it is a leprosy."

Isa 3:17 — "Therefore the Lord will smite with a scab the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will discover their secret parts."

Modern Corruption

The scab was diagnosed by an appointed examiner, never by the man himself; the live corruption is a religion of self-assessment, where every man is his own priest over his own sin and always pronounces himself clean.

expand to see more

Leviticus 13 is a standing rebuke to self-diagnosis. God did not leave the Israelite to decide whether the spot on his arm was nothing; He gave him a priest, a law, a waiting period, and a second look. Modern religion has reversed this entirely. The reigning assumption is that no one outside a man may name what is wrong inside him — that conscience is a private court with no appeal, that a sin is only a sin if the sinner agrees, and that any outside verdict is an intrusion. So the churches have quietly retired church discipline, elders no longer look on the plague, and the man with a spreading sore is congratulated on his honesty and sent home unexamined. Then the thing spreads, as Moses said it would, and what might have been dealt with as “but a scab” is at last a leprosy that costs a marriage, a ministry, or a soul.

Recover the appointed examiner. Scripture never flatters the sinner’s reading of himself: the heart is deceitful above all things, and he that trusteth in his own heart is a fool. God gave His church the ministry of the word and the office of elder precisely so that sin might be looked upon by a lawful eye and named for what it is. That is not cruelty; it is the mercy the leper never got until he was brought. And the priest of Leviticus was a shadow: the great High Priest looks on the plague of the heart, and He alone can pronounce clean not by finding no spot but by taking the uncleanness upon Himself. The man who submits to examination now has a Physician; the man who examines himself and acquits himself has only a spreading sore and a good opinion.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A crust upon the skin; in the law, the small symptom that must be brought to the priest and looked upon twice.

expand to see more

Scab — Saxon sceabb, Norse skabb, akin to Latin scabies, roughness.

Hebrew sappachath / mispachath, the scaly eruption of Leviticus 13.

The man does not judge it; he is brought unto the priest (Lev 13:2).

Seven days, then a second look — the verdict turns on whether it spreads (Lev 13:6–8).

Isaiah sets the scab where the ornament was, upon the crown of the proud (Isa 3:17).

Usage

"It is but a scab — the verdict of the priest, not the opinion of the patient."

"A spot that spreads is no longer a spot; that is why the law required a second look."

"Where the daughters of Zion wore their ornament, the LORD promised a scab (Isa 3:17)."
